cases.question: In an ordinary Indiana landlord-tenant possession case, what opportunity does the occupant have to present defenses before possession is ordered? Find and open relevant statutory text and an Indiana appellate opinion. Write a 150–220 word research note explaining what support and legal weight the opinion provides, which factual and procedural features limit its usefulness, and what remains unresolved. Distinguish preliminary possession from final resolution where the sources do. Identify source dates and links. Use at most eight source calls. Exclude emergency procedures. Use plain paraphrases unless quoting exact wording. If evidence is incomplete, say so without inventing authority.

message.content: Your ordinary possession question is in hand — pulling the statute and a matching appellate opinion.
Those searches were too narrow — broadening to the ejectment and possession statutes.
Found the opening filing provision — now locating the companion procedure on defending possession.
I've confirmed occupants get a show-cause hearing — now finding an appellate opinion that applies that procedure.

Research note — ordinary possession opportunity to be heard (emergency procedures excluded):

The retrieved ordinary ejectment/possession statute provides that after a plaintiff affidavit claiming entitlement and unlawful retention, the clerk issues an order directing the occupant to appear to dispute the affidavit or explain why possession should not transfer. The hearing may occur no earlier than five business days after service, and the order must advise the occupant that supporting affidavits may be filed, supporting testimony may be presented at the hearing, a written undertaking to stay delivery may be filed, and nonappearance can lead to a possession judgment for the plaintiff. This supports a pre-order opportunity to present defenses in the preliminary-possession phase, separate from any later final judgment, though the text read here alone does not fully detail trial, damages, or final merits procedures.

An indexed text-match search for that section returned, among others, Darrell E. Johnson v. Linda J. Larkins, Ind. Ct. App., filed 2023-06-27, docket 22A-EV-02844, listed as unpublished, and I-65 Plaza, LLC v. Indiana Grocery Group, LLC, filed 2021-03-31, listed as published. The opinion texts were not opened within the source-call limit, so no holding, reasoning, weight, facts, or preliminary-versus-final distinction can be reported from them, and a mention alone does not establish a holding.

Unresolved: what defenses succeed, burden at the show-cause hearing, undertaking/bond practice, and final resolution scope remain unverified.

result.heading: Action for ejectment or recovery of possession of real estate; plaintiff's affidavit
result.text:
Sec. 1. (a) This section applies to all actions:
(1) in ejectment; or
(2) for the recovery of possession of real estate.
(b) At the time of filing a complaint or at any time before judgment, a plaintiff may file with the clerk of the court in which the action is filed or pending an affidavit stating the following:
(1) The plaintiff is entitled to possession of the property described in the complaint.
(2) The defendant has unlawfully retained possession of the property described in the complaint.
(3) The estimated value of the property described in the complaint.
(4) The estimated rental value of the property described in the complaint.
[Pre-2002 Recodification Citation: 32-6-1.5-1.]

result.heading: Order to appear; order to show cause; requirements
result.text:
Sec. 2. (a) Upon the filing of an affidavit described in section 1 of this chapter, the clerk shall issue an order for a time fixed by the judge directing the defendant to appear to controvert the affidavit or to show cause why the judge should not remove the defendant from the property and put the plaintiff in possession. The order to show cause must direct the time within which the order must be served on the defendant and set forth the date, time, and place for the hearing, which may take place no earlier than five (5) business days after the date of service on the defendant.
(b) The order to show cause must state the following:
(1) The defendant may file supporting affidavits with the court.
(2) The defendant may appear and present supporting testimony at the hearing on the order to show cause.
(3) The defendant may file with the court a written undertaking to stay the delivery of the property under this chapter.
(4) The judge may issue a judgment of possession in favor of the plaintiff if the defendant fails to appear at the hearing.
[Pre-2002 Recodification Citation: 32-6-1.5-2.]
